title: Self-Attention — 7 Learning Questions
subtitle: Topic: Self-Attention and Contextual Representation Learning · Subject: Transformers and LLM Architecture. Seven exact questions with only leading Layer labels omitted, balanced A–D choices and seven distinct SVG teaching scenes.
hero:
SELF-ATTENTION · VISUAL OVERVIEW

Every token can use context from other tokens

One token forms a query, compares against visible keys, then gathers a weighted mixture of their values. Context changes its representation.

questions.stem: What is Self-Attention in Artificial Intelligence, and how does it allow each word or token in a sequence to gather information from other tokens within the same sequence?
questions.figure:
TOKEN RELATIONSHIP CONSTELLATION

Each word gathers information through learned attention links

Visual takeaway: Each query token gets its own distribution of attention weights. A token is not forced to treat every other token equally.
options: Self-attention passes a token through the network without comparing it with other tokens in its sentence. That preserves its original representation but misses relationships from the context.
Self-attention lets each token compare itself with other allowed tokens in the same sequence and combine useful information from them to build a context-aware representation.
Self-attention assigns every word a fixed meaning from a dictionary and prevents nearby words from influencing it. Learned embeddings and context can change representations.
Self-attention first sorts all the words alphabetically so similar words stand together before it computes representations. Transformer attention does not require rearranging the sentence.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Imagine a board-game rule that says, “Move the red piece after it reaches the bridge.” To understand what “it” refers to, the model needs information from other words in the same instruction. Self-attention allows a token to compare itself with relevant tokens and combine their information. That produces a context-aware representation. A mask can limit which positions are visible, so not every Transformer uses exactly the same attention pattern.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: B. Self-attention compares each token with tokens in the same sequence and uses learned weights to combine their information. This produces context-aware representations. Different attention masks decide which positions a token is allowed to see.

questions.stem: How does Self-Attention differ from traditional Attention Mechanisms and sequential processing methods such as RNNs and LSTMs, and why is it a fundamental building block of Transformer architectures?
questions.figure:
RNN CROSS ATTENTION AND SELF ATTENTION

Three mechanisms: recurrent state, cross-attention, self-attention

Key distinction: Self-attention derives Q, K and V from one sequence. RNNs propagate state step by step; cross-attention can compare one sequence against another.
options: Self-attention requires every output token to search a separate encoder sequence for context. That describes cross-attention, while self-attention works within one sequence.
Self-attention reads each token in order and carries one hidden state to the next step. That is a common RNN or LSTM processing pattern.
Self-attention prevents direct token comparisons and uses only fixed-width convolution filters to combine nearby words. Transformers instead use learned attention relationships between positions.
Self-attention relates tokens in one sequence, allowing Transformer training to compare many positions together, unlike recurrent methods that depend on sequential hidden-state updates.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Picture a long set of instructions for assembling a telescope. An RNN normally processes steps in sequence and passes information forward through its hidden state. A Transformer uses self-attention to connect information across the instruction text, including distant steps. The Query, Key, and Value representations come from the same sequence. During training, many token interactions can be calculated in parallel. Self-attention does not mean unlimited memory or that every token may see the future: masks still control visibility.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: D. Classic encoder-decoder attention may use queries from one sequence and keys/values from another. In self-attention, all three come from the same sequence. Unlike RNNs and LSTMs, Transformer self-attention can calculate positions together during training, while adding direct token-to-token interaction paths.

questions.stem: How does Self-Attention understand relationships between words in a sentence, such as determining what the word "it" refers to in "The animal crossed the road because it was frightened," and how does context influence the representation of each token?
questions.figure:
PRONOUN COREFERENCE ATTENTION SPOTLIGHT

Which noun does “it” refer to? Context guides the signal

Interpretation: A model may use “frightened” to favor “animal” over “road.” Attention alone is not a proof of model reasoning or a reliable explanation by itself.
options: Self-attention can give the word “animal” more weight when representing “it,” because “frightened” and the sentence context suggest which noun the pronoun refers to.
Self-attention must link “it” to “road” because “road” is the closest earlier noun. Word distance alone does not determine which reference makes sense in a sentence.
Self-attention must choose “animal” because it is the first noun, regardless of the rest of the sentence. Learned relevance depends on context rather than a first-noun rule.
Self-attention replaces “it” with a fixed dictionary definition before reading the other words. That would miss how the pronoun refers to something already mentioned.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Look at the sentence: “The animal crossed the road because it was frightened.” What was frightened? Most readers understand that it was the animal, not the road. A self-attention head can learn to connect “it” with “animal” while also using clues such as “frightened.” The model combines information from other tokens to represent “it” in context. Attention weights are learned signals, not a guaranteed explanation of every decision, but they help build contextual understanding.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: A. In this sentence, 'frightened' makes 'animal' a plausible antecedent for 'it'. An attention head may assign more weight to the animal token as part of its contextual representation. Attention weights are learned and are not definitive explanations of linguistic reasoning; multiple heads and layers contribute.

questions.stem: How does Self-Attention mathematically transform input embeddings into Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) matrices, calculate token-to-token similarity scores, apply scaling and softmax normalization, and generate contextualized token representations using the formula softmax(QKT/√dk)V?
questions.figure:
QKV MATRIX MULTIPLICATION AND SOFTMAX

Scaled dot-product attention turns comparisons into weighted values

Math: Q=XWq, K=XWk, V=XWv. Use QKᵀ/√dₖ for scores, apply masks if needed, softmax each row, then multiply by V. Heatmap values are illustrative.
options: The model first adds all token embeddings to obtain a single score, then selects the largest value. That loses the separate Query-Key relationships needed for normal self-attention.
The model calculates relevance using Values alone and averages every row without normalization. In standard self-attention, Query and Key create the scores used for weighting Values.
The model projects input embeddings into Q, K, and V, scales Query-Key scores, uses Softmax on allowed positions, and combines Value vectors into contextual outputs.
The model uses token position numbers as Queries, multiplies scores by Keys without normalization, and ignores learned projections. Positions cannot replace the normal attention calculations.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Imagine a message saying “The red ferry arrives at pier six.” The model starts with an embedding for each token. Learned matrices turn those embeddings into Queries, Keys, and Values. Each Query compares with Keys, producing scores for possible connections. Scaling controls score size, and Softmax turns them into weights. The weights combine Values to create a new representation for each token. The formula softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V summarizes these operations. A mask can block positions when required.
questions.sourceStem: How does Self-Attention mathematically transform input embeddings into Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) matrices, calculate token-to-token similarity scores, apply scaling and softmax normalization, and generate contextualized token representations using the formula \(\operatorname{softmax}(QK^T/\sqrt{d_k})V\)?
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: C. From inputs X, learn projections Q=XWq, K=XWk, V=XWv. The similarity matrix QKᵀ compares each query with all keys; dividing by √dₖ prevents scores becoming too large. Row-wise softmax turns scores into weights, and multiplying by V produces contextualized vectors. Masks exclude forbidden positions before softmax.

questions.stem: How can a Self-Attention layer be implemented from scratch using Python and PyTorch, including learnable projection matrices, matrix multiplication, attention weight calculation, optional masking, and visualization of the resulting token-to-token attention matrix?
questions.figure:
PYTORCH QKV PROJECTION AND CAUSAL HEATMAP

Implement learned projections, optional masking, and attention weights

self_attention.py · PyTorch
import math, torch
from torch import nn

torch.manual_seed(7)
class SelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.q = nn.Linear(dim, dim, bias=False)
        self.k = nn.Linear(dim, dim, bias=False)
        self.v = nn.Linear(dim, dim, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x, causal=False):
        Q, K, V = self.q(x), self.k(x), self.v(x)
        scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1)
        scores = scores / math.sqrt(K.shape[-1])
        if causal:
            n = x.size(-2)
            allowed = torch.ones(n, n, dtype=torch.bool, device=x.device).tril()
            scores = scores.masked_fill(~allowed, float("-inf"))
        weights = scores.softmax(dim=-1)
        return weights @ V, weights

x = torch.randn(1, 4, 8)
out, attention = SelfAttention(8)(x, causal=True)
print(out.shape, attention.shape)
print(attention[0].round(decimals=2))
Token-to-token attention

Heatmap is illustrative; the code prints its actual random-initialized weights.

Hands-on: The snippet creates Q/K/V with trainable matrices, calculates attention, and masks future positions when requested. No pretrained model is needed.
options: PyTorch can calculate attention by sorting tokens according to their position numbers and copying one fixed vector into each output, without learning any Q/K/V projections.
PyTorch can learn Q, K, and V projections from input vectors, calculate scaled attention scores with optional masks, apply Softmax, and combine Values into outputs.
PyTorch must download a complete pretrained language model before any attention layer can work. A small attention block can also start with newly initialized projection weights.
PyTorch gives every token pair the same attention weight regardless of the input text. That prevents it from learning which other tokens provide useful context.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Suppose you are testing a tiny model on spacecraft-docking instructions. Begin with token vectors in PyTorch and create three nn.Linear layers for Q, K, and V. Calculate scaled Q–K scores, apply a mask if needed, then use Softmax and multiply by V. A heatmap of the resulting attention matrix shows which input positions received more weight. The values are learned during training; the matrix is useful for debugging, although it does not tell the whole story of a prediction.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: B. A basic PyTorch implementation uses trainable nn.Linear projections for Q, K, and V, computes Q @ K.transpose(-2,-1) / √dₖ, optionally masks forbidden positions, normalizes with softmax and multiplies by V. The resulting matrix contains one attention distribution per query token.

questions.stem: How does Self-Attention behave differently in Bidirectional Transformers such as BERT and Causal Transformers such as GPT, including attention masks, information visibility, positional encoding, multi-head projections, and the influence of context length on token representations?
questions.figure:
BERT VERSUS GPT VISIBILITY HEATMAPS

Visibility matrices: full context or past-only context?

Architecture: Bidirectional attention can use both sides of a token in the input. Causal decoding forbids future tokens. Heads learn different projections, and longer context increases full-attention cost.
options: BERT hides all words to the right when reading input, while GPT reads future output words during generation. Those visibility rules reverse their usual attention patterns.
BERT and GPT use the same visibility mask and differ only in the size of their token vocabulary. Their training objectives and attention directions are also different.
Neither BERT nor GPT needs position information because attention alone knows the order of words. Both model families need some way to represent token positions.
BERT commonly uses bidirectional attention over its input; GPT uses a causal mask that blocks future positions while it predicts the next token in sequence.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Imagine reviewing an unfinished newspaper headline. A BERT-style model can examine words on both sides of a hidden word when learning or understanding the text. A GPT-style model instead predicts what comes next using only earlier tokens. The difference comes from attention masks: bidirectional versus causal. Both models also use position information and multiple attention heads. As the context grows, the model can consider more history, but attention and memory costs grow too.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: D. A bidirectional encoder such as BERT usually allows a token to use both earlier and later input positions. A causal decoder such as GPT prevents attention to future tokens, preserving autoregressive prediction. Both rely on positional information and multiple attention heads; increasing context length increases the available information and attention cost.

questions.stem: How can Self-Attention be optimized for large-scale Transformer models, including reducing quadratic computational complexity, managing KV caches during autoregressive inference, applying FlashAttention and sparse attention patterns, and evaluating the trade-offs between memory usage, processing speed, and long-context information retrieval?
questions.figure:
FLASHATTENTION TILING KV CACHE AND SPARSITY

Long-context optimization: tiles, cache reuse, and sparse patterns

Trade-off: FlashAttention is exact full attention with less memory traffic, not a subquadratic algorithm. KV caching helps decoding, while sparse patterns reduce work but can miss relevant tokens.
options: FlashAttention reduces memory traffic with tiles; KV caching reuses past values during decoding, while sparse patterns trade some connections for speed.
FlashAttention removes every pairwise calculation, while KV caches eliminate all memory needs during model training. Neither technique makes the entire attention system cost-free.
Sparse attention keeps the exact connections of dense attention while using fewer comparisons. Skipping selected connections generally changes what information each token can see.
KV caching deletes all earlier tokens after generation starts, making decoding independent of its context. A cache normally keeps reusable information from earlier positions.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Imagine an engineer searching through a huge software error log with an assistant. Full self-attention can be expensive because many token pairs may interact. FlashAttention handles calculations in efficient tiles, reducing memory movement while preserving exact attention. During word-by-word generation, KV caching reuses earlier keys and values. Sparse or sliding-window patterns reduce selected connections, which may save resources but can miss distant details. The goal is a useful balance between speed, memory, and information coverage.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: A. Ordinary full self-attention scores all token pairs, giving O(n²) score interactions. FlashAttention reorganizes exact attention into IO-efficient tiles, reducing memory traffic rather than eliminating quadratic arithmetic. KV caching reuses previous keys/values in causal inference. Sparse patterns reduce interactions but may miss distant dependencies. Evaluate speed, memory and retrieval quality together.
